description: BodyMed Hub, the system a physiotherapy clinic runs on: what it replaced, every module, a tour of the demo, the architecture, how it shipped and the four hardest decisions.

architecture.lede: Patients and staff use one application, and it talks to the service that owns each job.

services.name: Stripe
services.role: Checkout, Connect direct charges to each therapist’s own account, webhooks

timeline.lede: Planned from August 2026. The first piece shipped on 25 September, and the clinic went live five weeks later.

events.label: Shifts, email templates, appointments and rebook

dives.lede: Four problems where the obvious answer was wrong, or not available.

items.title: Paying self-employed therapists directly
items.problem: The therapists are self-employed. A payment for an appointment with one of them is their money, not the clinic’s, so it has to reach their own account.
options: One clinic account that pays therapists monthly
items.chose: Direct charges on each therapist’s own Stripe account. Stripe refused Express accounts that pay their own fees, which ruled that option out.
items.tradeoff: A saved card belongs to one therapist’s account, so saved cards work per therapist. A refund bug needed a fix, and then a repair of older records.

items.title: Never selling one time twice
items.problem: The Hub, clinic staff and the answering service can all book the same slot, and Cliniko has no webhooks and no locking.
options: Pay, then book from the webhook
items.chose: Pay, then book from Stripe’s webhook, with short-lived holds, a HELD block in the diary, a re-check after payment, and rebook or refund if the time has gone. “Authorise, book, capture” came too late before launch, and authorisations only last about 7 days.
items.tradeoff: A patient can pay for a time that someone else takes a moment later, so the Hub has to put that right by itself. A fix on 4 November 2026 closed a gap where a crash in the middle of a booking could leave it unfinished.

pipeline.caption: Pay, then book. Every step that can fail has a defined way out.

steps.title: Hold the slot
steps.detail: Before the patient pays, the server re-checks the time with the diary and holds it for 30 minutes, so two people can’t pay for the same slot. Phone pay links and waitlist offers hold a time for 2 hours.

steps.title: Take payment
steps.detail: Stripe Checkout, with the card saved for the cancellation policy. Every call that moves money carries an idempotency key.

steps.title: Claim the webhook event
steps.detail: Stripe retries webhooks. Each event is claimed once.

exit.then: Nothing changes. One appointment, one charge.

steps.title: Re-check the slot
steps.detail: Someone may have booked it by phone while the patient paid.

exit.then: Payment kept. Link to pick another time, refunded automatically after 7 days.

steps.title: Look before creating
steps.detail: If an earlier attempt already made the appointment, use that one instead of making a duplicate.

exit.then: Stripe retries for up to two hours. Then a full refund, an email, and an alert to the clinic.

steps.title: Confirm
steps.detail: Save the booking record, send the confirmation. The page polls for this status.

items.chosen: Pay, then book from the webhook

items.title: A fair waitlist without webhooks
items.problem: Cliniko has no webhooks, so nothing tells the Hub when a time opens up. When one does, more than one patient may want it.
items.chose: The Hub checks for open times every 5 minutes in working hours and offers each one to one person at a time. The rules below decide who, and when.

rules.value: A patient waiting for a named therapist first, then whoever has gone longest without an offer, then whoever joined first.
2 hours, and it always closes 60 minutes before the slot.
No automatic offers under 3 hours’ notice.
2 places on the list, 1 offer a day and 4 a week. Paused after 3 offers not taken. A place expires after 60 days.
The slot is held while they pay.
Rebook, or an automatic refund after 7 days.

items.tradeoff: Checking every 5 minutes means a freed time can wait a few minutes before anyone hears about it, and a time less than 3 hours away is never offered automatically.

items.title: Sign-in strong enough for refunds, on any laptop
items.problem: Staff can refund patients, so sign-in has to be strong. But not every laptop in the clinic has Face ID.
items.chose: Passkeys, plus approved computers for a laptop with no Face ID. A new browser waits for an approver, so access to someone’s inbox alone can’t move money.
items.tradeoff: A new computer can’t be used until someone approves it.

built.statement: Built with AI coding tools. I owned the product decisions with the clinic, the architecture (8 written decision records), reviewing and testing every change, and running it in production.
built.detail: Before launch I wrote the requirements, a failure modes and effects analysis of everything that could go wrong with money and bookings, a test plan, a go/no-go checklist and a runbook. The production code is private because it is tied to the clinic’s accounts.

lines: **Live since 30 October 2026**, taking real bookings and payments every day at book.bodymed.ie.

**142 tests pass across 21 files** in the public demo. Its end-to-end tests check that a repeated webhook gives one appointment and one charge, that a slot taken mid-payment keeps the payment, and that an unused rebook is refunded after 7 days.

pending.intro: In the first 10 days after launch, against a matched window before it:
lines: **Appointments paid in advance went from 0% to 14.5%.** Payment moved from the end of the appointment to booking time.
**90% of new online bookings (43 of 48) came through the Hub.**
**Online booking volume held steady**, at 46 before and 48 after.

reflection: The first version refunded a patient straight away when their slot was taken while they paid. Patients preferred not having to pay twice, so since 3 November 2026 the payment is kept and they choose another time instead.
The dropdowns taught me the bigger lesson: the people who use a system every day know the job better than I do.
I’d give it more time. Twelve weeks was tight for something a working clinic depends on every day.
